prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: All eight opening ballots rank the optical lattice clock, and that is not why I keep it first. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift so that many atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which gives Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with very narrow linewidths and a favourable statistical signal-to-noise ratio at the same time. Ye's group then turned this into the most accurate and stable measurement devices that exist, at the 1e-18 level and below, with clock comparisons over millimetre height differences that test the gravitational redshift. Many-body (spin-exchange) physics inside the clock is now a research topic of its own. The results are well replicated: several strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks around the world agree at these levels, and comparisons are being run between laboratories and over fibre links. That reproducibility is what I look for before I call something a measurement tool. The two-person credit is clean, because Katori holds the concept and the first realisation, and Ye holds the demonstrated performance and the extension to many-body regimes. The impact reaches fundamental-constant tests, searches for dark matter, geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this could be read as the next step in a prize lineage rather than a new discovery: the comb (2005) and ion control (2012) were already recognised, and the clock may look like their continuation. A second reservation is attribution. The ideas of lattice trapping and the clock community are broader than two names; Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the Yb and Hg groups, as well as Hall's and Hänsch's earlier comb work, all matter. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so some colleagues may argue the full consequence is still ahead.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the lattice clock third and asks whether it is an instrumentation advance building on the 2005 comb prize rather than a new physical discovery; he places topological insulators first for conceptual originality.
responses.response: I disagree that instrument means lesser. Spectroscopy and precision metrology have produced several Nobel prizes because a new measurement capability changes which questions can be asked. The lattice clock is more than a refinement of the comb: the comb provides the counting of optical cycles, while the clock is a separate physical system whose accuracy rests on the magic-wavelength trick and on controlling many atoms. I do take his point that topological insulators are conceptually original, but the credit there (Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents) is more contested than for the clock, and I do not think the committee should fund that uncertainty when a cleaner two-person case exists.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock second behind the Higgs experiments and says the 2005 prize covered the comb and not the clock, but she asks how the committee should divide credit between ion clocks (the 2012 prize) and lattice clocks.
responses.response: I agree there is no real overlap with 2005. On ions, the 2012 prize was for manipulating single quantum systems, and the best ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) are neighbours, not predecessors, of the lattice approach; lattice clocks have an advantage in stability from many atoms probed at once. I would keep the citation worded around the optical lattice clock so the ion work stays outside it. I am more hesitant about her first choice. The Higgs case is scientifically very strong, but I see no way to choose three of four names from two collaborations of thousands that the committee can defend, and I would like to hear how she proposes to do it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first and atom interferometry second, as I do, but notes that priority among early atom-interferometer demonstrations (Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich-Chu, Bordé) is contested and that Chu's 1997 prize may make the committee reluctant.
responses.response: I agree with her on the order, and her point about contested priority is the reason I do not propose B025 as a second prize part. The sensitivity story is persuasive, but the credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu is less settled than Katori and Ye. I would hold B025 as the first alternative and have the committee examine the attribution before putting it in a prize.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the lattice clock second, and says the redefinition of the second is still pending, which could make recognition better timed later; he also notes the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I agree his caution on circuit QED after the 2025 prize is justified. On timing, I would not wait for the redefinition: the physics results already stand, the 1e-18 uncertainties have been reproduced, and a redefinition would be a consequence of this work and not its test. Waiting would carry a risk of a missed or contested attribution as the field grows.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How to weigh Katori's concept against Ye's performance and whether other contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) should affect the two-name credit.
I am relying on memory for the exact record uncertainty values and the status of the redefinition of the second; I have not checked them here.
Whether a second prize part is useful. Atom interferometry (B025) is attractive but its credit is contested.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred B048 configuration. A minor connection: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is associated with that environment at JILA; I have no joint work or financial tie to Ye or Katori. Separately, my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Göran Johansson works, which matters for B001 and not for the preferred configuration.
